lessons.title: Lesson 1: Knowing your customer and your message
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a target customer profile and one clear message for a business.
This lesson builds toward: For a real or practice small business, you will write a target customer profile and a one-sentence marketing message, saying who the customer is, what they need, and what you offer, for whom and why you.
Marketing works when it speaks to a specific person. A target customer profile describes your best customer: who they are, what they need, what worries them and where they spend time online.
Then write one clear message: what you offer, who it is for and why they should choose you. Example: "Veteran-owned mobile detailing that comes to your driveway in Fayetteville. Book in two minutes."
AI can help you brainstorm. Ask: "I run a mobile car detailing business. Describe three types of likely customers and what each one cares about." Pick the one that matches the customers you actually have or want, and edit it with what you know.
Step by step:
- Name the business and what it sells.
- Ask an AI assistant to suggest three customer types.
- Choose one and write a short profile: who, needs, worries, where online.
- Write a one-sentence message: what, for whom, why you.
Words to know:
- Target customer: the specific kind of person your marketing is aimed at.
- Profile: a short description of a person or group.
- Message: the main thing you want customers to know and remember.
Try it now: Pick a real or practice business. Use an AI assistant to brainstorm customer types, then write a one-paragraph target customer profile and a one-sentence message.
You can now write a target customer profile and a clear marketing message.

check.q: What does a target customer profile describe?
options: Every person who uses the internet
Your best customer: who they are, what they need, what worries them and where they are online
Your prices for the year
Your competitors' logos
check.why: A profile describes one specific kind of customer so your marketing speaks to them.

check.q: AI suggests three customer types for your landscaping business. Only one matches who actually calls you. What do you do?
options: Use all three in every post
Pick the most exciting one
Ignore the AI and post nothing
Choose the one that matches real customers and edit it with what you know
check.why: Pick the type that matches your real or wanted customers and add what you know.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Writing social media posts with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to draft five posts, then edit them so they are accurate and sound like you.
This lesson builds toward: Using an AI assistant and your customer profile, you will write five social posts of different types, each with a call to action, with every fact, price and date checked and no claims you cannot prove.
Good posts teach, show or invite. Mix them: a tip ("3 ways to keep your car's interior clean"), a behind-the-scenes photo, a customer story (with permission), an offer, and a question that invites comments.
Give the AI your profile and message, then ask: "Write five short Instagram and Facebook posts for this customer. One tip, one behind the scenes, one customer story, one offer, one question. Friendly tone, under 60 words each, with a call to action."
Always edit. Check every fact, price and date. Remove claims you cannot back up, like "best in the state". Make it sound like you, and never post a review or result that did not happen.
Step by step:
- Paste your customer profile and message into the AI assistant.
- Ask for five posts of different types with a call to action.
- Check each fact, price and date.
- Cut claims you cannot prove.
- Rewrite in your own voice.
Words to know:
- Call to action: the step you want the reader to take, like "Book now" or "Call today".
- Caption: the text that goes with a social media picture or video.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to draft five posts for your business using the prompt pattern above. Edit each one for facts and voice, and mark what you changed.
You can now draft social posts with AI and edit them to be accurate, honest and in your voice.

check.q: Which post is a "behind the scenes" post?
options: A photo of your team setting up for a job
A 20% off coupon
A question asking followers their favorite color
A customer's review
check.why: Behind-the-scenes posts show how your work happens.

check.q: An AI-drafted post lists a price you changed last month. What do you do?
options: Post it; customers will ask
Delete the whole post
Fix the price before posting
Add "prices may vary" and post it
check.why: Always check and correct every fact, price and date before posting.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Making graphics with Canva and AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a clean, on-brand graphic for each post using a free design tool.
This lesson builds toward: Using Canva's free plan, you will create an on-brand graphic for each post, using the same colors and fonts, few words and only images you have the right to use.
Canva has a free plan with templates sized for each social site. Search for the post type you need, such as "Instagram post", pick a template and replace the words and pictures.
Keep a simple brand: the same two or three colors, one or two fonts and your logo or business name on every graphic. Use few words on the image; the caption carries the details.
Use your own photos when you can; real pictures of your work build trust. If you use AI-generated images, do not make them look like real customers or results you did not deliver, and only use pictures you have the right to use.
Step by step:
- Open Canva and search for the template size you need.
- Pick a template and change the colors to your brand colors.
- Replace the text with a short headline.
- Add your own photo or a properly licensed image.
- Download it and save it with the post's name.
Words to know:
- Template: a ready-made design you change to fit your needs.
- Brand: the look and feel that makes your business recognizable.
- License: permission to use an image or other work.
Official sources:
- Canva
Try it now: Make a Canva graphic for each of your five posts using the same colors and fonts. Use at least one real photo of your work or product.
You can now create consistent, honest graphics for social posts with a free design tool.

check.q: Where should most of the details for a post go?
options: Packed onto the graphic
In tiny print at the bottom of the image
In a second graphic
In the caption, with few words on the image
check.why: Keep few words on the image; the caption carries the details.

check.q: You want a picture of a happy customer, but you have none. What is the honest choice?
options: Use an AI image made to look like a real customer
Use a photo of your own work or a properly licensed image
Copy a photo from another company's site
Use a stranger's photo from social media
check.why: Use your own photos or images you have the right to use, and do not fake customers.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Email, honesty rules and results

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing a marketing email that follows the law
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Draft a marketing email with AI that meets the main U.S. CAN-SPAM requirements.
This lesson builds toward: Given an offer for past customers, you will write a marketing email that meets the main CAN-SPAM requirements, with an honest subject line, a physical address and a clear unsubscribe option.
Email reaches people who already chose to hear from you, so it often sells better than social media. Only email people who gave you their address and agreed to hear from you.
In the United States, the CAN-SPAM Act sets rules for commercial email. According to the Federal Trade Commission, you must not use false or misleading header information or subject lines, you must identify the message as an ad, include your valid physical postal address, give a clear way to opt out, and honor opt-outs within 10 business days. You stay responsible even if someone else sends it for you.
Ask AI for a draft: "Write a short marketing email for [business] offering [deal] to past customers. Honest subject line, friendly tone, one call to action." Then add your address and unsubscribe link, and check the facts. Outside the U.S., check your own country's email and privacy rules.
Step by step:
- Ask AI for a short email with an honest subject line and one call to action.
- Check every fact, price and date.
- Make it clear this is an advertisement or offer.
- Add your valid physical postal address.
- Add a clear unsubscribe option and honor requests within 10 business days.
Words to know:
- CAN-SPAM Act: the U.S. law that sets rules for commercial email.
- Opt out / unsubscribe: a way for people to stop getting your emails.
- Subject line: the short title people see before opening an email.
Official sources:
- FTC: CAN-SPAM Act Compliance Guide for Business
Try it now: Use AI to draft a marketing email for your business. Edit it, then check it against the CAN-SPAM list: honest subject line, identified as an ad, physical address, unsubscribe option.
You can now write a marketing email with AI help that meets the main CAN-SPAM rules.

check.q: Who should be on your marketing email list?
options: Anyone whose email you can find
Email addresses you bought online
People who gave you their address and agreed to hear from you
Every business in your town
check.why: Only email people who gave you their address and agreed to hear from you.

check.q: Your AI draft has a great offer but no address or unsubscribe link. What do you do before sending?
options: Add your valid physical postal address and a clear unsubscribe option
Send it; those are optional
Add only your phone number
Send it from a friend's account instead
check.why: CAN-SPAM requires a valid physical postal address and a clear way to opt out.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Honest marketing: disclosures, reviews and AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Spot when an ad needs a disclosure and keep reviews and AI content honest.
This lesson builds toward: Given an ad, a review or AI-made content, you will identify when a disclosure is needed and keep reviews and testimonials honest, getting at least 4 of 5 cases right.
The FTC's Endorsement Guides say that if someone promoting a product has a connection to the brand, such as being paid or getting a free product, it must be disclosed clearly. The FTC suggests simple words like "Ad:" or "#ad" at the start, or "Paid post by [brand]".
Fake reviews are deceptive. Never write reviews for your own business, pay for fake ones or have AI generate them. Ask real customers for honest reviews instead.
Be careful with AI-made content: do not use AI to imitate a real person, invent testimonials or make claims about results you cannot prove. Rules change, so check the FTC's business guidance pages for the current details.
Words to know:
- Endorsement: a message where someone says they like or use a product.
- Disclosure: a clear statement of a connection, like "#ad" or "Paid post".
- Testimonial: a customer's statement about their experience.
Official sources:
- FTC: Endorsement Guides, What People Are Asking
Try it now: Review your five posts and email. Mark any that would need a disclosure (for example, a partner paid you or a friend promotes it for free product), and remove any claim or review that is not real.
You can now spot when marketing needs a disclosure and keep reviews and AI content honest.

check.q: When must a person promoting your product disclose it?
options: Only if they have over 10,000 followers
When they have a connection to your brand, such as being paid or getting it free
Never, if the review is positive
Only on email
check.why: The FTC says a connection like payment or a free product must be disclosed clearly.

check.q: Your shop has few reviews. A friend offers to have AI write twenty five-star reviews. What do you do?
options: Accept, since AI wrote them, not you
Post only ten of them
Pay a service to post them instead
Decline and ask real customers for honest reviews
check.why: Fake reviews are deceptive; ask real customers instead.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Measuring what works and improving
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a number to track for each post and use the results to plan next week.
This lesson builds toward: After a week of posts, you will choose one number to track for each post and use the results to plan next week, with a tracking sheet that has a goal number and a result for every post.
Every social platform and email tool shows basic numbers. Reach is how many people saw it. Engagement is likes, comments, shares and saves. Clicks show who went to your link. Conversions are the real goal: bookings, calls, sales or sign-ups.
Pick one main number per post based on its job: a tip post aims for saves and shares, an offer aims for clicks and bookings. Write them in a simple tracking sheet in Google Sheets or Excel.
After a week, look at what did best and do more of it. You can paste your numbers (no customer names) into an AI assistant and ask: "Which posts did best and what should I try next week?" You make the final decision.
Step by step:
- Make a sheet with columns: date, post, type, goal number, result.
- Choose one goal number for each post.
- After a week, fill in the results from the platform's insights.
- Ask AI to spot patterns, using numbers only.
- Plan next week: more of what worked.
Words to know:
- Reach: how many people saw your post.
- Engagement: likes, comments, shares and saves.
- Conversion: when someone takes the action you want, like booking or buying.
Try it now: Final task: build a tracking sheet for your five posts and your email, with one goal number each. Together with your profile, posts, graphics and email, this completes your one-week marketing kit.
You can now plan, create, check and measure one week of AI-assisted digital marketing.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Customer profile The profile is missing or describes "everyone". One paragraph on who the customer is, their needs, worries and where they are online. Every post and the email clearly speak to this one customer. Five posts Fewer than five posts, or a post has an unchecked fact or a claim you cannot prove. Five posts of different types, each with a call to action, with facts checked. The posts sound like the owner, not like a generic AI draft. Graphics Graphics are missing, crowded with words or use images you do not have the right to use. A clean graphic for each post with the same brand colors and fonts. Uses real photos of the business's own work. Marketing email The subject line is misleading, or the address or unsubscribe option is missing. Honest subject line, clear that it is an offer, physical address and unsubscribe option. Also says how opt-outs will be honored within 10 business days. Tracking sheet No tracking sheet, or no goal number per post. A sheet listing one goal number for each post and where to find the result. Results are filled in and next week's plan is based on them. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: Likes, comments, shares and saves
How many people saw the post
The cost of the post
The number of followers you started with
check.why: Engagement counts how people interact with a post; reach is how many saw it.

check.q: Your tip posts got the most saves this week, but offers got few clicks. What is a sensible next step?
options: Stop posting for a month
Delete the tip posts
Plan more tip posts and try a new offer next week
Post the same offer five times
check.why: Do more of what worked and adjust what did not.
